featuredTitle: First Steps for Newly Diagnosed Families
featuredContent:
The post-diagnosis process is the beginning of both an emotional and informative journey for families. Here are the first steps:

1. Acceptance and Emotional Support: Give yourself time. It is normal for this process to feel like a grieving period. Getting support from an expert psychologist increases the family's resilience.

2. Special Education Planning: Early intervention is the most critical step. Collaborate with experts to prepare an individual education program (IEP) tailored to your child's needs.

3. Health and Reporting: Ensure your child benefits from legal rights (supportive education, rehabilitation, etc.) by completing RAM (Guidance and Research Center) and hospital procedures.

4. Home Environment Arrangement: Simplify the home according to your child's sensory needs. Help them understand the daily routine using visual schedules.

5. Informing the Social Circle: Build the right support network by informing your close circle and relatives about the situation.

sections.title: What is Autism?
sections.description: A clear summary of what Autism Spectrum Disorder is, how it appears, and why it is called a "spectrum".
sections.content:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that can manifest itself with differences in social communication, behavior, and learning style from the early stages of development.

Why is it called a "spectrum"?
- Because symptoms and support needs can vary greatly from person to person.
- Some individuals may be independent with less support in daily life, while others may require more intensively structured support.

Common areas
- Social communication: initiating/maintaining reciprocal conversation, understanding gestures-facial expressions, establishing joint attention.
- Behavioral patterns: need for routine, repetitive behaviors, limited interests.
- Sensory differences: hyper/hypo-sensitivity to stimuli such as sound, light, touch, smell.

Important notes
- Autism is not a single "mold"; the strengths and challenging areas of two children with the same diagnosis can be different.
- Early and regular support (such as special education, speech-language therapy, occupational therapy/sensory integration) can strengthen the child's development and daily living skills.
- The goal is not to "eliminate autism"; it is to increase communication, support independence, reduce difficulties, and make family life sustainable.

sections.title: Education in Autism
sections.description: Educational planning with early intervention, in-class adaptations, and individualized goals.
sections.content:
Education in autism is carried out with a structured and individualized plan to support the child's communication, social interaction, play/learning, and daily living skills.

Basic principles
- Individualization: Goals are determined according to the child's developmental level, strengths, and needs.
- Consistency: Common goal language and similar methods between home-school-special education.
- Visual supports: Daily routine schedules, step-by-step instruction cards, "first-then" board.
- Structured learning: Clear start/end, short and understandable instructions, repetition, and generalization.

Commonly used educational approaches (general framework)
- Behavioral approaches: Teaching desired skills and reducing problem behaviors (e.g., ABA-based techniques).
- Developmental approaches: Strengthening social-communication skills through play and interaction.
- Class-based arrangements: Visual cues, breaking tasks into small steps, sensory regulation, facilitating transitions.

Practical checklist
- Set a measurable goal (e.g., "requesting", "turn-taking", "toilet routine").
- Integrate goals into the daily routine (short repetitions at home and school).
- Track progress with simple recording (with which cue did they succeed?).

Resources
- CDC: https://www.cdc.gov/autism/treatment/
- WHO: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders

sections.title: Social Communication
sections.description: Practical suggestions for supporting skills such as eye contact, joint attention, turn-taking play, and expressing emotions in daily life.
sections.content:
Social communication is not just talking, but a combination of many skills such as reciprocal interaction, turn-taking, reading cues, and sharing emotions. These skills may develop at different rates in children with autism.

Approaches that work in daily life
- Joint attention: The goal is to "share" what interests the child together (e.g., look at the toy → you look too → a short word/sign). This is the basis of communication.
- Eye contact: Without forcing; very short and natural contacts are targeted at motivating moments such as games, songs, bubbles, favorite objects.
- Requesting: "Wanting" increases communication. Create small opportunities for the child to want something (e.g., keep the biscuit in the box, wait for them to ask for help).
- Emotion awareness: Concepts such as "happy/sad/angry/surprised" can be reinforced with pictures, mirror mimic exercises, short videos, and simple emotion cards.
- Turn-taking and sharing: "My turn / your turn" games (throwing a ball, stacking blocks, drawing a card) strengthen social interaction.

Supports that facilitate communication
- Visual support: Picture routine, step-by-step instruction cards, "first-then" board.
- Simple and consistent language: Short sentence, clear instruction, routine expressions repeating the same words.
- Social stories: Explains difficult social situations (market, guest, playground) with short and concrete sentences; clarifies the expected behavior.

Goal: For the child to be able to express their own needs, ask for support when having difficulty, and establish small but sustainable social interactions.

sections.title: Therapy in Autism
sections.description: Skill development with speech-language, occupational therapy, behavioral, and developmental interventions.
sections.content:
Therapy in autism is not a "single method", but the joint planning of multiple supports (communication, sensory regulation, behavior, daily living skills) selected according to the child's needs.

Commonly used therapy areas
- Speech and language therapy: Comprehension/expression, reciprocal communication, alternative communication methods (sign, picture, device) included.
- Occupational therapy: Daily living skills (dressing, eating, self-care) and sensory regulation needs.
- Behavioral and developmental interventions: Skill teaching, supporting problem behaviors according to their function, strengthening play and social interaction.
- Social skill studies: Structured group or individual studies.
- Psychological support: Adapted therapy approaches in accompanying areas such as anxiety, emotion regulation (especially in older children/adolescents).

What does a good therapy plan look like?
- Goals are clear and connected to daily life (e.g., "requesting", "reducing difficulty in transitions").
- Home application is given to the family (short, sustainable).
- Progress is tracked with data and goals are updated.

Resources
- CDC: https://www.cdc.gov/autism/treatment/
- WHO: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders

sections.title: Sensory Integration
sections.description: Simple adjustments that can be applied at home and outside when there is sensitivity in senses such as sound, light, touch, and movement.
sections.content:
Sensory integration is the organization of sensory information from the environment (sound, light, touch, smell, movement, balance) by the brain. In children with autism, senses can sometimes work "too much" (hypersensitive) and sometimes "too little" (hyposensitive).

Common examples
- Sound: Overreacting to sounds like vacuum cleaner, crowd, bell, or conversely seeking very loud sound.
- Touch: Sensitivity to contact such as tags, seams, haircut, nail clipping.
- Visual: Bright lights, crowded image, screen sensitivity.
- Movement/balance: Constant need to rock/jump or avoidance of some movements.

Small adjustments that can be applied at home
- "Calm corner": An area with reduced noise, dim light, soft cushions.
- Preparation in advance: Short explanation + visual before going to a new environment (where, how long, what will happen).
- Gradual habituation: Short time + reward with the disturbing stimulus, slowly increasing the time.

Practical solutions outside
- Noise-canceling headphones or earplugs.
- Avoiding crowded hours (choosing quiet hours for the market/mall).
- Preferring tagless/comfortable fabrics in clothing selection.

Nutrition and texture selectivity
- It is more sustainable to progress with very small steps rather than a "big change at once" (steps like touching-smelling-licking-tasting).

Sensory supports are individual. The best approach is to observe which stimuli the child has difficulty with, reduce the triggers, and create safe spaces with a regular routine.

sections.title: Treatment in Autism
sections.description: The "treatment" approach in autism: education/therapy for core features, medical support for accompanying conditions.
sections.content:
Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition. Therefore, an approach such as "completely eliminating with a single treatment" is not scientifically correct.

However, support mechanisms proceed in 2 main branches:

1. Core developmental areas (Communication, Social Adaptation, Behavior)
- The main approach is special education, speech therapy, and occupational therapy. The goal is to maximize the individual's potential.

2. Accompanying conditions (Medical support)
- Autism is often accompanied by sleep problems, gastrointestinal problems, anxiety, attention deficit, or epilepsy.
- Medication support can be provided for these specific conditions (when necessary) under the control of Child/Adolescent Psychiatry or Neurology physicians.
- Medications do not "cure" autism, but they can increase the child's compliance with therapy (for example, learning accelerates when attention deficit decreases).

Important Warning: It is critical to stay away from alternative methods (diets, supplements, unapproved therapies) that are not evidence-based and promise a "definitive solution" and to always follow the physician's advice.
